hero.name: Mohan
hero.who: a 62-year-old retired railway officer in Lucknow who has lost his calm

story.b: For thirty-five years, Mohan's day had a shape. Railway office at nine, files till six, home by seven. Now, eight months into retirement in Lucknow's Aliganj, the days have no shape at all. He reads three newspapers and gets annoyed at all of them. He scolds the maid for being late, argues with his son on the phone about a new car, and checks his pension account twice a day. His wife Kamla says he has become a pressure cooker without a whistle. One evening at the park, his walking friend Iqbal seems completely calm, though his own knee surgery is next week. Mohan asks how. Iqbal shrugs and says he decided long ago what he was living for.

ask.q: Mohan wants the kind of calm Iqbal has. What is the most useful way to start?
o: Read every ancient text on calm before changing anything
Try a few simple, practical habits of mind in ordinary daily moments
Avoid newspapers and people so nothing can annoy him
ask.why: Calm is not something you only read about, and hiding from the world does not last. A few practical habits of mind, tried in ordinary moments, can steady Mohan far more than either. A philosophy works best when it is practised, not kept on a shelf.

chapters.take: Lasting calm comes from simple practices, tried in ordinary days.

story.b: Mohan thinks about Iqbal's words for days. One morning, sitting with his tea on the verandah, he realises he never decided what he was living for. He just chased the next thing. First a promotion, then a bigger flat in Aliganj, then a car, then his son's college seat. Each one felt good for a month. He takes an old visiting card and writes one sentence on the back. A good life, for me, is being useful, being kind at home, and being at peace with what I cannot control. It looks almost too simple. He keeps the card in his shirt pocket anyway. That afternoon a former colleague calls with an offer: a well-paid consultancy at a private logistics firm, five days a week.

ask.q: The consultancy pays well but takes five days a week. How should Mohan decide?
o: Take it, since more money and status are always good
Refuse it, since retired people should only rest
Check it against his own sentence about what a good life means
ask.why: Without a clear idea of a good life, Mohan would chase money and status by default, or refuse out of habit. His one sentence gives him a test. If the work fits what he is living for, he can say yes, or shape it until it does. If not, he can decline calmly.

chapters.take: Know what a good life means to you, or you will chase the wrong things.

story.b: Mohan's son calls to say the grandchildren will spend May in Lucknow. Mohan grumbles before he can stop himself. Two boys, cricket in the drawing room, cartoons at full volume, sticky hands on his newspapers. Kamla gives him a look over her glasses. That night, unable to sleep, he tries something he once read about. He quietly imagines the opposite: a May when the boys do not come, then years when they are too busy to visit at all. The house goes perfectly quiet in his mind. He feels a pang and stops, telling himself this is a gloomy way to think. But in the morning, the thought of a cricket ball in the drawing room sounds different. Almost welcome.

ask.q: Mohan worries that imagining a May without the boys is a gloomy habit. Should he keep doing it now and then?
o: Yes, briefly, because picturing a loss helps him value what he has now
No, because thinking about loss can only bring sadness
Only if he also plans ways to escape the noise
ask.why: The practice is not meant to make Mohan sad, and done briefly it rarely does. It reminds him how precious the noisy visit is, before it is gone. Avoiding all thought of loss keeps him grumbling, and escaping the noise misses the very thing he would miss most.

chapters.take: Picture losing what you have, briefly, and you will treasure it today.

story.b: Mohan has grown roses on his terrace for years, and this winter he enters the colony flower show for the first time. Within a week he is obsessed with winning. He checks the weather app five times a day and worries that the judges always favour the society secretary's garden. He snaps at Kamla for watering the pots wrong. Then he takes the card out of his shirt pocket and reads it again. At peace with what he cannot control. The weather is not his. The judges are not his. What is his is the compost, the pruning, the watering at six every morning, and how well he presents the flowers on the day. He sits down and rewrites his goal on the back of the card.

ask.q: Mohan badly wants the rose prize, but the weather and judges are out of his hands. What goal should he set?
o: Win first place, whatever it takes
Grow and present his roses as well as he possibly can
Skip the show, since he cannot control the result
ask.why: Mohan can only partly influence the prize, so aiming at it ties his peace to judges and weather. Skipping the show throws away the joy of it. A goal he fully controls, his own care and effort, keeps him trying hard without the result ruling his mood.

chapters.take: Aim for your best effort. That part, at least, is always yours.

story.b: Mohan notices how small inconveniences ruin his mood. A slow lift, a late newspaper, a hot afternoon. So he starts choosing a little discomfort on purpose. His doctor has already said regular walking is good for him, so he walks the two kilometres to the vegetable market instead of taking an e-rickshaw. He climbs the stairs to his third-floor flat. Once a week he skips his evening sweet. The first walk in the heat leaves him grumpy and thirsty, carrying bags of tomatoes and lauki. By the second week he enjoys it. Then his car goes to the workshop for two weeks, and his neighbour Verma complains endlessly about autos. Mohan barely notices. An e-rickshaw ride home now feels like a small luxury.

ask.q: Kamla asks why Mohan walks to the market when an e-rickshaw costs only twenty rupees. What is the best reason?
o: To save twenty rupees on every trip
To prove he is fitter than his friends
Small chosen discomforts make him tougher and make comforts feel special
ask.why: Saving money is a side benefit, and proving himself to friends is about ego. The real point of small chosen discomforts is that they build toughness, so future hardships shake Mohan less, and an ordinary e-rickshaw ride starts to feel like a treat again.

chapters.take: Choose a little discomfort on purpose, and hard days will shake you less.

story.b: At a family wedding in Sitapur, a cousin mentions the land near the highway. Mohan sold his share of their father's plot eleven years ago, in a hurry, for a fraction of what it is worth today. The cousin means nothing by it, but the old regret floods back. On the drive home, Mohan replays the whole sale. The broker's smile, the papers he signed without reading closely, the price he could have asked. Kamla sees his jaw tighten and puts her hand on his arm. He has relived that day perhaps a hundred times. It has never once brought the land back. At home he sits at the dining table with the card from his pocket and a fresh sheet of paper.

ask.q: The old regret about the land sale is back. What should Mohan do with it?
o: Go over the sale again to find exactly who misled him
Accept it cannot change, write down what he learned, and turn to what is next
Avoid that cousin so the topic never comes up again
ask.why: The sale is finished, and replaying it adds fresh pain to an old event. Hunting for someone to blame keeps the wound open, and avoiding the cousin only hides from it. Accepting what happened and noting the lesson lets Mohan put his energy into what he can still shape.

chapters.take: The past cannot change. Learn from it, then turn to what is next.

story.b: The colony flower show comes and goes. Mohan's roses win nothing, and he is surprised to find he does not mind. They were the healthiest he has ever grown. He took the consultancy for two days a week, not five, because that fit the card in his pocket. In May the grandsons came, broke a flowerpot and a window latch, and left behind a quiet house that he missed for days. He still walks to the market and still takes the stairs. The land in Sitapur rarely crosses his mind now, and when it does, he remembers the lesson and lets it go. Kamla says the pressure cooker has found its whistle. Iqbal, back on his feet after surgery, just smiles.

chapters.take: Calm is not luck. It is a handful of small practices, kept every day.
